questions.q: What are the three kinds of control flow elements every SSIS package is built from?
questions.explain: Every control flow is made of containers (structure), tasks (units of work), and precedence constraints (the connectors that order and condition execution).

questions.q: Which of these is a container, not a task?
questions.explain: For Loop, Foreach Loop, and Sequence are containers — structures that hold other tasks and containers. The other three options are all tasks.

questions.q: What determines the order in which two connected tasks run, and the conditions under which the second one runs?
options: The Toolbox category they're listed under
questions.explain: The connector between two items in a control flow is a precedence constraint — it sets execution order and the conditions (success, failure, completion) under which the next item runs.

questions.q: Can containers be nested inside other containers?
options: Yes — a Foreach Loop container can hold another Foreach Loop container, and so on to any depth
No — SSIS only allows one level of container nesting
Only Sequence Containers can be nested; loop containers cannot
Only if both containers use the same enumerator type
questions.explain: Integration Services' architecture explicitly supports nesting containers to multiple levels — a control flow can include several layers of nested containers.

questions.q: If a task has no incoming precedence constraint, when does it run?
options: Never — every task requires an incoming precedence constraint
Only after every other task in the package has finished
Only if its container is disabled
questions.explain: A task with no incoming constraint has nothing to wait on, so it starts running as soon as the package begins execution.
